newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan minister says received cash from oil trader.
newsitem.headline: Japan minister says received cash from oil trader.

text.p: Japan's new Finance Minister, Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, acknowledged on Tuesday that a political faction he headed had received political donations from an oil trader at the centre of a tax evasion scandal.
But Mitsuzuka, who was named finance minister in Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new government last week, said the donations were legal and proper and did not constitute a bribe.
Opposition politicians seized on the issue as an opening for their first attack on Hashimoto's new administration.

Mitsuzuka said his faction, the second biggest within the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), received a total of 6.5 million yen ($58,500) from millionaire oil wholesaler Junichi Izui over a two-year period starting in 1992.
The cash was funnelled through fund-raising groups run by the faction, he told a news conference.
"We were not asked to do anything (in return for Izui's political donations)," he said. "It was not a donation of that sort."
The 60-year-old Izui, owner and sole employee of oil wholesaler Izui Oil Co, was arrested last Thursday on charges he evaded 310 million yen ($2.79 million) in taxes.
The scandal involves a series of complex deals involving Izui and oil giants Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd and Mitsui Mining Co.
Apart from Mitsuzuka's group, a dozen politicians had received cash from the oil trader, Kyodo news agency quoted unnamed investigation sources as saying.
Kyodo said the Osaka oil dealer also wined and dined about 100 bureaucrats from the powerful Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) and the Finance Ministry.
Izui handed over to authorities a notebook in which he had recorded banquet dates, the names of 16 politicians and amounts of political donations, Kyodo said.
Although Prime Minister Hashimoto said he had not received cash from the oil trader, he ordered a review of all political donations he had received.
"As far as I know, I received none," Hashimoto told reporters
The main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) said it wanted a parliamentary debate on the issue.
"New doubts have surfaced. This issue should be debated at least from the political ethics perspective," Shinshinto official Kansei Nakano told reporters.
Japan has been rocked by a series of scandals involving overly cosy or improper links between government officials and businessmen.
In one case last year, then Finance Minister Masayoshi Takemura docked his own pay over a scandal involving a senior ministry official taking improper gifts from business contacts.

One of the biggest political scandals of recent years was the 1980s Recruit stocks-for-favours affair that was seen as a symbol of the excesses of the nation's "bubble economy" era of inflated land and share prices.

Many of Japan's senior politicians, bureaucrats and business executives were believed to have received shares of Tokyo-based job information company Recruit Cosmos before the stock was listed and its price jumped.
The scandal caused a political furore that led to the downfall of Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita in June 1989.
